Thank you for noticing this point. We agree that this aspect of the figure could be clearer, thus we have
modified it for the revision. To quantify d-prime performance across training, we used a rolling window of 40
trials in which each data point reflects the average d-prime over a set of consecutive trials (e.g., trials 1–40,
2–41, etc.). As a result, even the first point plotted on the original graph (“trial 1”) incorporated performance
across the initial several trials. Because mice often acquire discrimination rapidly within the first few trials,
this can create apparent differences early in the curve. We have updated the figure and figure legend so that
the axis starts with trial 20, and each point represents a rolling window that includes 20 trials before and 20
trials after (see revised Figure 5F).

(20 trials/ block) compared to controls to reach the performance criterion. Now we include the average
number of blocks and SEM in the figure legend to clarify the extent of the delay (Figure 5G). This represents

Thank you for raising this important point. All hM4Di mice did eventually learn the Go/No-Go task and
reached the 85% accuracy criterion, demonstrating that they were able to acquire the discrimination
capacity. However, their d-prime values reported the difference between the Hit rate and the False alarm

R4: 4. Throughout the paper (for example: abstract lines 37-39, introduction lines 75-77, introduction

glutamatergic and cholinergic neurons. For example, in the abstract lines 37-39 “Within the BF nuclei,
glutamatergic (vGlut2BF) neurons relay cholinergic input to modulate behavior”- does this mean BF
glutamatergic neurons also release acetylcholine? If so, can references be provided?
We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and thoughtful comments. To avoid redundancy and improve
clarity, we have removed the repeated the reference to “cholinergic basal forebrain” throughout the
manuscript when not specifically relevant. Regarding the statement that vGlut2BF neurons “relay
cholinergic input,” our intention was not to imply that these glutamatergic neurons themselves release
acetylcholine. Rather, we meant that their activity is modulated by cholinergic signaling within the basal
forebrain microcircuit. We agree that the term “relay” could be misleading in this context, so we have
revised the text to clarify that vGlut2BF neurons integrate cholinergic modulation to influence behavior. The
revised phrasing makes it explicit that these neurons are glutamatergic and do not co-release acetylcholine
(see line 38).

Can the authors provide clarification and provide references?
We appreciate to reviewer for this helpful request for clarification. Yes, we are referring to the basal
forebrain GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons receiving cholinergic input from BFCNs. To make this
clearer, we have revised the text to specify that these populations receive fast cholinergic synaptic input
from cholinergic neurons within the basal forebrain. We have also added references to support this point
(Patel et al. 2019; Yang et al. 2014; McKenna et al. 2021).
The introduction should be expanded to mention differences between BF regions (if any). There are

neurons in the different BF regions would be helpful to the reader. Moreover, the focus of this current
paper was in the hDB. The introduction should be expanded to include studies that have focused
specifically within hDB.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to better contextualize the anatomical and functional
heterogeneity of the basal forebrain (BF). In response, we have expanded the introduction to describe the
distinct roles of major BF subregions, including the globus pallidus/substantia innominata (GP/SI) and the
horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB), emphasizing their differential involvement in sensory, reward,
and aversion-related processing. We now highlight the rationale for focusing on the HDB in this study, as it is
uniquely positioned to modulate olfactory perception through its reciprocal connectivity with the olfactory
bulb. Additionally, we cite studies showing that lesioning or silencing neuronal populations in the HDB
15
impairs olfactory-guided behavior, supporting its functional relevance in odor-driven associative learning.
These additions help establish the HDB as a distinct and appropriate target for investigating basal forebrain
contributions to valence encoding and sensory modulation (see line 96-103).
R4: 5. The discussion section of the paper would be enhanced if authors first focused the discussion
more specifically on the hDB- i.e., what are the inputs and outputs of the hDB? What is the neuronal
composition of the hDB? Can any of these factors influence the authors findings? Although a
discussion of the BF in general is appreciated, the authors should first focus on the brain region of
interest described in the current study (hDB).
We appreciate this thoughtful suggestion to improve the focus of the discussion. In the revised manuscript,
we have now expanded the section discussing the horizontal limb of the diagonal band (HDB). Specifically,
we describe that the HDB is composed of cholinergic, GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons (e.g., Gracia-
Llanes et al., 2010; Záborszky et al., 1986), and that it receives inputs from regions such as the olfactory
bulb, piriform cortex, hypothalamus, and brainstem modulatory centers. The HDB projects prominently to
the olfactory bulb, where it modulates olfactory processing and perception (Niedworok et al., 2012; Gracia-
Llanes et al., 2010). Additionally, lesion or silencing studies have demonstrated that disrupting HDB activity
alters olfactory-mediated behaviors (Nunez-Parra et al., 2013; Moss et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2015;
Paolini and McKenzie, 1993). We have also added a more thorough introduction describing the anatomical and
functional properties of the HDB to provide better context for our findings.

Thank you for this request for clarification. The Euclidean distance measures how different the activity
patterns of the neuronal population are when responding to different stimuli. Specifically, we create a vector
representing the mean population response to each odor, with each element corresponding to the activity of
an individual neuron. We then calculate the Euclidean distance between these vectors, which quantifies the
overall dissimilarity between the two response patterns. Larger distances indicate more distinct
representations of the odors across the recorded neurons. We have added this explanation to both the
Result and Method section to improve clarity. (See line 253-262, Method line 933-939).

between population activity vectors evoked the odors. We compared the distance between the same odor
before and after conditioning, or between different odors in the same session. This metric captures how

12. In distinct parts of the BF, cholinergic afferents co-express vGlut3 (Barabas et al, 2024). Can the
authors expand on vGlut2 vs. vGlut3 BFCNs in the discussion and what the potential implications are?
We appreciate the reviewer raising this point, and agree it is important to clarify the differences between
vGlut2 and vGlut3 expression in the basal forebrain. vGlut2 and vGlut3 mark distinct glutamatergic
populations. Specifically, vGlut2 does not overlap with ChAT (McKenna et al., 2021), indicating that vGlut2+
neurons are non-cholinergic glutamatergic projection neurons. In contrast, vGlut3 is often co-expressed
with ChAT (Barabas et al., 2024), reflecting a unique subset of cholinergic neurons capable of glutamate co-
release. We expected that vGlut3 expressing neurons will act the same as the cholinergic neurons in the
basal forebrain, however we feel this would require experimentation beyond the scope of this study.
13. In the discussion, the authors mention multiple subtypes of vGlut2 BF. What are these subtypes
and what factors distinguish the different subtypes of vGlut2 BF neurons? How would this impact the
author's findings?
We appreciate this inquiry, given it’s an outstanding question we also have. Our data show that some vGlut2
BF neurons are odor responsive while others are recruited specifically after associative learning, suggesting
this population is functionally heterogeneous. However, molecular markers that clearly define distinct
subpopulations of vGlut2 BF neurons are still being established. For example, McKenna et al. (2021)
identified that subsets of BF vGlut2-tdTomato neurons co-express either the calcium-binding protein
calbindin (Calb) or calretinin (Calr). Whether there are neurons that co-express both proteins remains
unclear, and the functional roles of these subpopulations have not yet been tested.
Future experiments using these molecular markers could help determine whether specific subtypes are
preferentially involved in encoding odor identity versus associative or emotionally salient reinforcement.
Such studies could clarify whether the observed heterogeneity in our recordings reflects distinct functional
specializations within the vGlut2 BF population. We have added topic area and future directions to the
discussion in the revised manuscript.
